guidance: Food scraps and leftovers are biodegradable and belong in the wet/organic bin, where they can be composted rather than sent to landfill.
tip: Keep a small lidded bin near the kitchen counter so wet waste never mixes with dry waste at the source.

guidance: Garden and plant waste is organic and compostable, and should go with wet waste rather than general dry trash.
tip: Dry, brown garden waste (like dead leaves) composts faster when mixed with a little wet, green waste.

guidance: Used tea bags and coffee grounds are organic matter and belong in the wet/organic bin; most are compostable.
tip: Check if the tea bag has a plastic mesh or seal — remove that part (dry waste) before composting the rest.

guidance: Paper that is heavily soiled with food or oil (like the base of a greasy pizza box) cannot be recycled and should go with wet/organic waste, not dry recyclables.
tip: Tear off and recycle any clean, unstained part of the box separately — only the greasy section goes with wet waste.

guidance: Clean paper and cardboard are recyclable and belong in the dry waste bin.
tip: Flatten boxes before disposal — it saves space and makes sorting at collection centres faster.

guidance: Glass bottles and jars are recyclable dry waste. If broken, the glass is still recyclable but poses a cut risk during handling.
tip: Wrap broken glass in newspaper or a sealed pouch labelled 'glass' before placing it in the dry bin, so it's handled safely.

guidance: Clean plastic, metal cans, and foil are recyclable and belong in the dry waste bin.
tip: Give containers a quick rinse — food residue can get an entire batch of recyclables rejected at the sorting facility.

guidance: Batteries contain heavy metals and chemicals that can leach into soil and water. They must never go in regular bins.
tip: Look for a designated battery drop-box at electronics stores or your municipal hazardous-waste collection point.

guidance: Expired or unused medicines can contaminate water supplies if thrown in regular trash and should be treated as hazardous waste.
tip: Many pharmacies accept expired medicines for safe disposal — ask before throwing them out at home.

guidance: Paints, chemicals, and aerosols are hazardous and can be flammable or toxic; they require specialised disposal, not regular bins.
tip: Let paint cans dry out completely before disposal where required by your local guidelines — check before doing this.

guidance: Sanitary and personal hygiene waste should be wrapped separately and treated as hazardous/biomedical waste, not mixed with recyclables.
tip: Wrap sanitary waste in paper (not plastic) before disposal, as many municipalities specifically request this.

guidance: Electronic devices and accessories contain metals and components that need specialised e-waste recycling, not regular dry waste.
tip: Most brands and electronics retailers run e-waste take-back programs — check before assuming it has to go in the trash.
